questions.prompt: What does Continuous Integration (CI) mean in practice?
options: A quarterly manual code review conducted by a release manager
Every developer merges small changes into a shared branch frequently, and an automated process immediately verifies each change
Keeping every developer's code in a separate branch that never merges
A once-a-year audit of all Salesforce metadata
questions.explain: CI means merging small changes frequently and having an automated process verify each one immediately, catching problems the moment they're introduced.
questions.distractorExplain: Option A describes a periodic manual review, not an automated, continuous process -- the defining feature of CI is that verification happens automatically on every merge, not on a schedule set by a person.

questions.prompt: Why is a Salesforce deployment fundamentally different from deploying a typical web application to a server?
options: A Salesforce deployment moves metadata into an already-running, live org rather than shipping a compiled binary or container to a provisioned server
Salesforce deployments never involve any kind of automated testing
Web application deployments and Salesforce deployments work identically in every respect
Salesforce has no concept of a target environment at all
questions.explain: There's no compiled binary in a Salesforce deployment -- metadata moves directly into a live, already-running org, which is exactly why validation and testing matter as much as they do throughout this course.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Before Apex classes and triggers can be deployed to a production org, tests must cover at least ________ percent of the total Apex code in that org.
questions.explain: Salesforce enforces a 75% org-wide Apex coverage minimum (with per-class/trigger floors too) before allowing a production deployment that includes Apex.

questions.prompt: A pipeline needs to deploy to production and must run every test in the org except tests belonging to installed managed and unlocked packages. Which --test-level value does this?
options: RunSpecifiedTests
RunAllTestsInOrg
RunLocalTests
RunRelevantTests
questions.explain: RunLocalTests runs every test except those from installed managed/unlocked packages, and is the default Salesforce applies to production deployments that include Apex.

questions.prompt: A validation job returned by sf project deploy validate is intended to be quick-deployed within what window before it expires?
options: 24 hours
10 days
90 days
It never expires
questions.explain: A validation job ID from sf project deploy validate is valid for 10 days from when the validation started.

questions.prompt: Match each pipeline design principle to what it actually means.
right: Running the same step twice with the same input produces the same result both times
A manual or alternate route kept available when an automated shortcut (like a delta deployment) misbehaves
Stopping a pipeline immediately and clearly at the first failure rather than limping forward
Keeping the time between a change and its pipeline result short enough for the result to still be useful
questions.explain: Fail fast means stopping immediately on the first problem. Idempotent means repeat-safe. A fallback path is the manual full-deploy option kept available if a delta deployment misbehaves. A fast feedback loop keeps pipeline results useful to the developer who just made the change.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about release automation, per this course.
options: Release automation replaces 'a person remembers to do this' with 'this happens automatically when a defined event occurs'
Most teams keep a human approval gate specifically in front of the production release step, even once everything before it is fully automated
Release automation makes manual Change Sets illegal to use
Teams that get release automation right often move toward smaller, more frequent releases
GitHub Actions environments with required reviewers are one way to implement a deliberate approval gate
questions.explain: Release automation replaces manual triggering with automatic triggering, but a human approval gate typically still guards the actual production release. It doesn't make Change Sets illegal -- the real argument is about cost scaling, not legality. Automation also tends to push teams toward smaller, more frequent releases, and GitHub Actions environments with required reviewers are the concrete mechanism for the approval gate.

questions.prompt: In a GitHub Actions workflow file, what does the 'uses:' keyword do in a step?
options: It executes a raw shell command directly on the runner
It invokes a reusable, pre-built action, such as actions/checkout@v4
It deletes the workflow file after the run completes
It sets the workflow's trigger event
questions.explain: 'uses:' calls a packaged, reusable action; 'run:' is the keyword that executes a raw shell command instead.
questions.distractorExplain: Option A describes 'run:', not 'uses:' -- the two keywords are the two distinct ways a step can do work, and they are not interchangeable.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: on sf project deploy start, the flag that tells the CLI how many minutes to wait for a deployment to finish before returning control is ________.
questions.explain: --wait (or its short form -w) controls how long the CLI waits for a deploy to complete; its default is 33 minutes, which CI pipelines often raise for large deployments.

questions.prompt: Why can't a GitHub Actions runner authenticate to Salesforce using sf org login web?
options: sf org login web is deprecated and no longer exists
GitHub Actions blocks all outbound traffic to Salesforce domains
A CI runner is a disposable machine with no browser a human can interact with, so interactive login can't work there
sf org login web only works against sandboxes, never production
questions.explain: Interactive browser-based login requires a human to respond to a prompt -- something a disposable, non-interactive CI runner has no way to provide, which is exactly why the JWT Bearer flow exists for CI.

questions.prompt: Match each JWT-flow GitHub secret to what it holds.
right: The Consumer Key from the org's Connected App
The full contents of the private key file, including the BEGIN/END lines
questions.explain: SF_CLIENT_ID holds the Connected App's Consumer Key, SF_PRIVATE_KEY holds the private key file contents, SF_USERNAME holds the dedicated integration user's username, and SF_INSTANCE_URL holds the org's My Domain URL.

questions.prompt: Why does a delta-deployment pipeline need its checkout step configured with fetch-depth: 0?
options: fetch-depth: 0 is required before the Salesforce CLI can be installed
A default shallow clone contains only the latest commit with no history, and sfdx-git-delta needs full Git history to diff two commits
It makes the Apex test suite run faster
It disables branch protection for the duration of the run
questions.explain: sfdx-git-delta computes its diff by comparing two actual Git commits; a shallow clone (the GitHub Actions default) doesn't include the prior commit, so fetch-depth: 0 pulls full history for the diff to work against.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about quality gates in a Salesforce CI/CD pipeline.
options: A quality gate is only real if a failure is wired to an actual consequence, such as blocking a pull request merge
GitHub branch protection rules are what give a failing check the power to actually block a merge
A static analysis gate should fail the build on every single finding regardless of severity, to be maximally strict
The platform's own 75% Apex coverage minimum is enforced by Salesforce itself, independent of any pipeline configuration
A gate with no enforcement behind it is really just a dashboard
questions.explain: A gate only matters if failure has a real consequence, and branch protection is what turns a failing check into an actual merge blocker. Failing on every trivial finding (rather than using a severity threshold) trains teams to ignore the gate, which is the opposite of the lesson's recommendation. The 75% coverage rule is enforced by the platform itself, separate from anything a pipeline configures. And a check with no enforcement is correctly described as just a dashboard, not a gate.

questions.prompt: What is PMD's role inside Salesforce Code Analyzer?
options: PMD is a separate, unrelated competing product
PMD is one of the underlying engines Code Analyzer bundles, specifically configured with rules for Apex and Visualforce by default
PMD only works on JavaScript files, never Apex
PMD replaced Code Analyzer and the latter no longer exists
questions.explain: Code Analyzer runs multiple engines, and PMD -- defaulting to the apex and visualforce languages -- is the one doing most of the actual Apex rule-checking.

questions.prompt: What does the GitHub Actions step condition if: failure() do?
options: It deletes the failed job's logs automatically
It runs the step only if an earlier step in the same job failed
It retries every failed step up to three times automatically
It runs the step on every single run, success or failure
questions.explain: if: failure() scopes a step -- typically a notification -- to only execute when a prior step in the same job failed, exactly the behavior wanted for an alert you don't want firing on every successful run.

questions.prompt: Put these JWT key-pair rotation steps in the correct order, from first to last.
items: Generate a new RSA key pair
Upload the new certificate to the Connected App
Update the SF_PRIVATE_KEY GitHub secret with the new private key and confirm authentication still works
questions.explain: Rotation generates the new key pair first, uploads the new certificate to the Connected App, confirms the updated secret authenticates successfully, and only then deactivates the old certificate -- so the pipeline is never left unable to authenticate mid-rotation.

questions.prompt: What does Salesforce provide as a native, built-in way to undo a completed metadata deployment?
options: A one-click 'Undo Deployment' button in Setup
A --rollback flag on sf project deploy start
Nothing -- there is no built-in rollback; recovery uses git revert and/or a pre-deployment metadata snapshot instead
An automatic 24-hour grace period that reverts any deployment
questions.explain: Salesforce has no native one-click rollback for a metadata deployment. Once a deploy succeeds, the org's metadata is simply in its new state -- real recovery relies on reverting the offending Git commit and redeploying, or restoring from a retrieved pre-deployment snapshot.

questions.prompt: What happens to existing records when a pipeline deploys a new required field to production?
options: The field is automatically populated on every existing record
Nothing -- a metadata deploy doesn't touch existing records at all; populating the field is a separate, deliberate data operation using tools like sf data import tree
All existing records matching that object are deleted
The deployment is automatically blocked until every record has a value
questions.explain: Metadata deploys move structural definitions, not records -- a new field appearing on an object doesn't by itself change any existing row's data; moving actual record data is a separate operation entirely.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: every newly created unlocked (2GP) package version starts with the status ________, regardless of whether a human or a CI job triggered its creation.
questions.explain: A new package version is always marked beta at creation; promotion to released status, making it installable into production orgs, is a separate, deliberate action.

questions.prompt: In the course's case study, a trigger references a custom field that nobody included in the same pull request. Where does the pipeline actually catch this, and why not earlier?
options: The static analysis (PMD) step catches it, since missing dependencies are exactly the kind of pattern PMD's rules look for

The delta-deploy step catches it with a component-level error naming the missing reference -- static analysis alone wouldn't, since a missing-dependency problem isn't a code-quality pattern PMD checks for
Nothing in this pipeline, as designed, could ever catch this kind of problem
Only a human reviewer reading every line of every pull request could catch this
questions.explain: A missing-dependency error is a deploy-time failure, not a static-analysis pattern -- it surfaces when the deploy step tries to resolve the reference and fails, which is exactly why a pipeline needs both static analysis and a real deploy/validation step, not one in place of the other.
